en: We shall now explain the measurement by means of a cord (*rajju-samāsa*). Having fixed a gnomon (*śaṅku*) in level ground and having drawn a circle with a cord equal in length to the gnomon, one fixes two gnomons at the points where the shadow of the tip of the [central] gnomon falls upon the two intersecting lines; that line is the east-west direction (*prācī*). Having doubled the distance between those two points with a cord and made loops at both ends, one fastens the loops to the two gnomons, pulls [the cord] toward the south, and fixes a gnomon in the middle; likewise toward the north—that is the north-south direction (*udīcī*).

He makes two loops at the ends of the cords. There are marks for the hips, the shoulders, the rubbing-out lines (*nirañchana*), the measurements, and the breaking of the compound. He drives stakes into the eastern ends and into the hips and shoulders. Having fastened the loops to the two stakes and having grasped them with the rubbing-out line, they carry it toward the south-eastern direction. Likewise on the north. On the other side, they proceed by reversing the order. That is the method everywhere. Having repeated the measurement four times, he makes a fine mark; that is the rubbing-out line (*nirañchana*). The remainder is the diagonal cross-measurement.

Having repeated [the measurement] by half the dimension, one makes a mark at the sixth repetition; that is the removal of the [previous] mark. The remainder of the crosswise measurement is the peg for the square of half the dimension. For the long square, it is as prescribed in the Śāstra. And the same applies to the "cart-mouth" [shape].

By this, the measurements of the *prāgvaṃśa* hall and the altar (*vedi*) are explained, as well as the measurement of the *śālā*. Therein, the northern line is like the eastern one. And the same applies to the *sadas*.

The [space] beyond the measure is immeasurable (aparimita). Regarding the measurement, the scripture is the authority for both reduction and increase. And as for the yoga, we shall explain that "the other third part to the south. The space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires is divided into six or seven equal parts; having divided it into three, one marks the third part from the rear toward the south. Upon that [mark], the fire is placed. Having reversed [the direction], the utkara mound is placed to the north.

Alternatively, having made a square with equal sides in the eastern half by means of this cord, which is one-third of the interior [measurement], the fire-altar is placed at the hip; by reversing it, the rubbish-heap (utkara) is at the northern shoulder.

The measurement for a chariot-sized [altar] is as follows: there, the pole (īṣā) is one hundred and eighty-eight finger-breadths; the axle (akṣa) is four hundred; the yoke (yuga) is eighty-six; and the pin (śamyā) consists of four sets of eight. In the case of the ancestral altar (paitṛkī), having made a square measuring two persons on each side, the pegs are placed in the middle of the cords; that is the method.
The *karaṇī*, the *tatkaraṇī*, the transverse-measuring cord (*tiryaṅmānī*), the side-measuring cord (*pārśvamānī*), and the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayā*) are the [five] cords.

(3) When the transverse-measuring cord is one foot (*pada*) and the side-measuring cord is three feet, its diagonal cord is ten-fold (*daśakaraṇī*). (4) Likewise, when the transverse-measuring cord is two feet and the side-measuring cord is six feet, its diagonal cord is forty-fold (*catvāriṃśatkaraṇī*). (5)

The measurement of a *yuga* and the measurement of a *śamyā* have been taught through observation. (6) Knowledge of the area [is as follows]: the diagonal cord (*akṣṇayā rajju*) of a long rectangle produces both that which the transverse side-measure and the lateral side-measure produce when they are separate.
(7) The diagonal cord of a square is the double-maker (*dvikaraṇī*). (8)

One should increase the *karaṇī* by one-third; that [third] is increased by its own fourth part diminished by one twenty-fourth—this is the "special" (*saviśeṣa*) [measure], which is the "special" (*viśeṣa*). 9. The measurement across is two *karaṇīs*, and its diagonal cord is three *karaṇīs*. 10. The third *karaṇī* is explained by this. As for the division of the measurement: the third of a *karaṇī* is a ninth part. Three ninth parts constitute a third *karaṇī*. 11.
In the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice, it serves the purpose of the commencement; the third *karaṇī* serves the purpose of the combination (*samāsa*).

The method of combining squares of equal dimensions has been stated. Regarding the combination of squares of different dimensions: one should cut off from the larger [square] a portion equal to the side of the smaller [square]; the diagonal cord of that [portion] combines both—this is the combination. One who wishes to subtract a square from a square should cut off from both sides as much as he wishes to subtract, drive in stakes, and having made a side-measure, he applies there a diagonal cord equal to that side-measure; this is the cutting-off in the combination, and this is the *karaṇī* for the subtraction.

One who wishes to make a long rectangle into a square should cut off a transverse portion from the middle and divide one of the two resulting parts; he should place the other part to the east and to the south, and fill up the remainder with an additional area. The method for reducing its size has already been explained. If it is excessively long, one should repeatedly cut off transverse portions, and having combined them into a single unit, one should apply the remaining area as appropriate; this is one method of combination.

One who wishes to make a square equal [in area] to a long rectangle should cut off a diagonal section from the middle, divide that [section], and place one part in the front and one in the north; Vyāsa says that if it is unequal, one should adjust it as appropriate. (4) A measurement other than a square is determined by specific instruction. (5) A side of two units has an area of four units; a side of three units has an area of nine units; a side of four units has an area of sixteen units. (6)
As many units as there are in the length of the cord, so many squares are there; one should combine them.

(7) By half the measure, a quarter-measure is prescribed; by a third, a ninth part; by a fourth, a sixteenth fraction. (8) This is the reduction; the teaching concerning it has been stated previously in the Śāstra. (9)

As long as the cord remains [of its original] measure, there is a reduction when it is extended. (10) One desiring to make a square into a circle should drop the cord from the center to a corner and draw around it from the side; whatever remains in excess, one should draw the circle together with a third part of that—this is the method. (11) One desiring to make a circle into a square should divide the diameter into fifteen parts and remove two; the remainder is the measuring-cord (*karaṇī*). (12)
The fire-altars are: the Droṇacit, the Ratha-cakra-cit, the Kaṅka-cit, the Prauga-cit, the Ubhayataḥ-prauga, and the Samūhya-purīṣa.

1. Regarding the Droṇa: having made a square as large as the fire-altar itself—including its wings and tail—with the droṇa serving as the tenth part, some say the stalk (*vṛnta*) is one-tenth of that. Having cut off portions repeatedly by that tenth part, having combined them into a single whole, and having extracted [the shape], one should construct the entire fire-altar in that form and place it either in front or behind. The same applies to the circular altar (*maṇḍala*). 2. In the case of the circle as well, it is the same.

3. Having made a square twice the size of the *prauga* fire-altar—including its wings and tail—as it exists there, that fire-altar is defined by the peg at the middle of the front-side cord and the two pegs at the hips.
4. Having made a long rectangle of exactly the same dimensions as the *prauga* on both sides, the pegs are placed at the middles of the cords; that is the method of construction. 5.

One desiring to make the *prauga* a square should cut off a portion from the middle facing forward, transpose it, and place it on the other side; one should then combine it with the long rectangle—that is the method of construction.
If it is a *prauga* altar on both sides, one should cut off the middle transversely and join the parts together as previously described.

By this same method, the joining of three-cornered altars is explained, as well as that of five-cornered ones; for those with one corner, one cuts off from the *prauga*; for those with two corners, one cuts off from a square.
Regarding the subsequent [altars], we shall explain up to the one-hundred-and-one-fold altar by means of the accumulation of *puruṣa*s.
The first fire becomes double and then triple; this is the summary of all [the fires] (2). It becomes twenty-one-fold; this is the repetition of the *puruṣa* (3).
In the repetition of the *puruṣa*, having made a square as large as the fire—including its wings and tail—with that [area], one should place a measure of a *puruṣa* within it (4).

Having divided the whole into fifteen parts, one should combine two [parts] into a single unit; that is the *puruṣa*. By a fivefold division, the *bṛhatī* becomes a foot-measure through its tenth part. Alternatively, having cut off a *puruṣa* from both sides by a fifth part and having combined the five parts, one should remove a third [of that] and place it upon that which is of the measure of a *puruṣa*; this is another method.

A division into fifteen parts is eight *aṅgulas* (8); five *aratnis* are ten *vitastis*, which is two hundred *aṅgulas*; this is a *puruṣa*. From this [measurement], a foot (*pada*) is twelve *aṅgulas* (9). Alternatively, having cut off a seventh part from both sides of the *puruṣa*, having combined the seven parts, and having subtracted one-seventh of an *aṅgula*, one should apply it to the measurement of the *puruṣa*; this is another method (10).
There is no compound formation for words such as *nāra*, *tīr*, and *vitasti* when joined with a numeral, according to the scriptural authority (*śruti*).

For example, we shall explain how the measurement of the fire-altar bricks increases. Furthermore, the *yākaraṇī* (the line-drawing cord) contracts fourteen steps (*prakrama*) and three-sevenths of a step; this is the step in the one-hundred-and-one-fold altar.
Or, in the second case, having fixed a step within seven steps, one part of a step is [measured] by the seventh part of that;
or one part of a step is [measured] by the seventh part of a step.
Thus, from the one-hundred-and-one-fold [altar], there are five [methods].

There is no increase for the *nāntaḥpāti* and the *gārhapatya*; their womb remains exactly as it was. For according to the Śruti, "The womb does not expand along with the fetus that has been born," there is an absolute prohibition against expansion. (6) As many square units of equal size as one intends to combine into one, those [units] are to be one less; they are doubled across and increased by one on one side, and thus it becomes a triangle. An arrow serves as its [measuring] cord; one performs that [measurement]. (7) We shall explain the expansion of the altar according to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). (8)

The rope that brings together eleven *uparava* pits and ten axle-lengths of a chariot—its twenty-fourth part is a *prakrama*. Having measured out the altar (*vedi*) with that, and having cut off twelve finger-breadths from the front, he fixes a marker (*śaṅku*) to the east of the *yūpāvatiya* marker; upon that he erects the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). Or, as it is stated in the scripture, "half on each side within the altar," they are half-measures.
Some [teachers] say that the first and last [verses] are like the original;
this very Śikhaṇḍinī is the altar.
And there are verses on this point:
One should fashion the characteristic marks at two cubits; the head should be three cubits.
Behind the head it should be one span, and in the front half, exactly one cubit.
At one and a half cubits there should be a loop, and the altar should be like that of the Full Moon sacrifice.
One who knows the numbers, knows the measurements, is skilled in drawing level lines and marking out boundaries, and is an expert in cord-work and inquiry, shall become a wise man on level ground.
There is nothing equal to water for leveling, nor can there be any other standard than the wind.
Nothing other than the cord is straight; nothing other than the cord is distant from the error above.
The knower of yoga, who understands the divisions of the measuring lines (karaṇīs), employs the cross-measures for all purposes and the side-measures as well, being ever-diligent in his ritual acts.

One who understands divisions through knowledge of the treatises and possesses curiosity for other sciences should always acquire insights from artisans and architects. [The measure is] six finger-breadths in circumference and twelve finger-breadths in height.
One should especially make the stake (*śaṅku*) old and free from blemishes;
the mallet (*mudgara*) should likewise be made of *khadira* wood and measure two spans (*vitasti*).
Therefore, the stake is to be driven [into the ground] by means of that [mallet], and thus its acceptance [is prescribed]. 7–8.
On one side, however, a peg made of *khadira* wood—straight, sharp, and of equal length—should be prepared by those skilled in cord-work; they should drive half of it into the ground.
At a *haviḥ-yajña*, it should be one *prādeśa* in length and marked with the aforementioned characteristics.
A spike with three heads should be made; one should also bury half of it.
It should be a square mallet, sixteen finger-breadths in length, unperforated, beautiful, and fashioned from the heartwood of a tree.
A cord that is undecayed, without knots, fine, even, smooth, hairless, and exceeding the required measure should be prepared for the sacrifice by one desiring success.
It is prescribed as being made of hemp, flax, or bamboo.

The rope used in the sacrificial rite should have loops at both ends and be made of three strands. Kātyāyana declares that the rope should be made of muñja grass mixed with śaṇa fibers, or alternatively, it may be made of unbroken kuśa and balbaja grasses.
One should fashion nine marks; one should fashion three in each of the [three] groups.
The ninefold noose is said to be the supreme measure of the assembly hall (sadas).
Then there is the fifteen-fold, another twenty-one-fold, and further the triple.
In the Soma sacrifice, this measurement of the cord is twelve pāśas long;
the diagonal across the foot should be the same.
In the Sautrāmaṇī, the altar should be measured out according to that same method as in the Soma sacrifice.
Just as one would hold up a lamp in the water when light is obscured by dense mist or clouds, so long as there is the perception of darkness;
likewise, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and whatever else is designated as a "thing" [are held up]. 18.
Having understood all that from the scriptures, the performers of sacrifice achieve success in the sacrifice.
One should practice yoga in such a way that the mind does not diminish, nor does it increase, and so that the vision finds delight.
The *khara* for the eastern fire should be square and one *aratni* in size;
that of the western [fire] should be shaped like a chariot wheel, and that of the southern [fire] like a half-moon.
The *khara* for all these fires should be provided with three girdles (*mekhalā*).

Twelve finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width, the fiber of the lotus stalk is wrapped six times around; it should be similar to the hair of a calf one year old or three years old. 22–23.
Three three-year-old barley grains are said to equal half a mustard seed;
one should know that two mustard seeds make one barley grain, and five mustard seeds make one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
The measurement of a finger-breadth consists of six barley grains placed side by side.
Twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) make one cubit (aratni), and twelve finger-breadths make one span (vitasti).
Here, the measure of a fathom (vyāma) is one hundred minus four [finger-breadths].
The measure of a man, however, is indeed one hundred and twenty [finger-breadths].
But when gold is not explicitly mentioned for the purpose of the gold fragments (hiraṇya-śakala), that sacrificial procedure is explained as being accomplished by means of a *kṛṣṇala* alone.
A *kṛṣṇala* is a measure of three *yavas*; beyond this, it is made of copper.

He should give half a *māṣa* for gold, and seventy-three *suvarṇas* for the *bahusuvarṇaka* rite; furthermore, having learned from the master (*sthapati*), the man of knowledge should give three thousand [gold pieces] for other designations.
Just as a goldsmith increases [the work] further through practice,
so too [the clay] diminishes through drying and baking; the brick [should be made] with thirty-two parts [of excess],
therefore a wise man should make it larger than the required measurement while it is still wet.

Those who, without knowing the true essence of the Śulba-sūtra, desire to construct the altar for the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice performed at the end of the Soma-pressing, are like those who attempt to split a mountain with their fingernails.
Having practiced the staff-line and the cord up to the fifth [measurement], the marking of the half occurs at the sixth.

In the same way, elsewhere as well, the horizontal measurement may be according to one's preference. (32) The cord should be of whatever length [is required], and the arrival-point (āgama) should be of that same measure;
the peg (śaṅku) should be half the length of the arrival-point, and the mark (nirañjana) should be half of that. (33)

In the rite of establishing the sacred fires (ādhāna), one should make a step of one square; in the Soma sacrifice, it should be two squares; and at the fire-altar, the wise sacrificer should make a step of three squares.
[The asterisms] Kṛttikā, Śravaṇa, Puṣya, and the interval between Citrā and Svāti—these are auspicious.
This is the form [of the altar] from the eastern direction when the sun has risen to the height of a yoke; fifty pebbles are to be placed behind, seventy-three in front,
and fifteen, five, and seven to be given in the south.

The portion for the twenty-four sides of the *śaṃsya* should be drawn out by fourteen [units]; likewise, the *narya* part should be drawn out by eight times two [units]. Then, having extended it by thirty [units], one should remove a third.
At nine and a half *aṅgulas* to the north of Agni, one should then draw the center.
The eastern chord, situated in the middle, shall consist of nineteen units;
leaving out the northern half, it extends as far as the south of the fire-altar (khara) for one who is wise, possesses secret mantras, and is free from the defects of the measuring-line. 38.
This work on the art of measurement by the great-souled Kātyāyana is completed.
Thus ends the Kātyāyana-Śulbasūtra.
